s1: Hi, I'm Doctor Helix! Welcome to the DNA lab. Every living thing, from you to a tulip, follows a recipe written in a molecule called DNA. Drag the glowing helix to spin it. Ready to zoom into your own body and read the recipe?
s2: Let's shrink! You are made of about thirty seven trillion cells. Each cell has a nucleus, the control room. Inside it are chromosomes, and inside those, DNA. Drag the zoom slider and watch the sizes change. Each step is far smaller than the last.
s3: Here's a puzzle. Stretched out, the DNA in one cell is about two metres long, yet it fits in a nucleus much smaller than a grain of sand. The trick is packing. DNA wraps around protein spools called histones, then coils again and again. Slide to pack it!
s4: Humans have forty six chromosomes, arranged as twenty three pairs. You got one chromosome of each pair from each parent. Click two matching chromosomes to pair them up. The last pair decides sex: X X usually means female, X Y usually means male.
s5: Now the star: the double helix. Two long strands twist around each other like a spiral ladder. The sides are sugar and phosphate. The rungs are pairs of bases. One full turn has about ten rungs, and the whole thing is only two nanometres wide. Click the parts!
s6: The rungs follow strict rules. A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. So if you know one strand, you know the other! Build the matching strand by clicking the correct bases. This rule is how cells copy DNA perfectly before they divide.
s7: A gene is a stretch of DNA that holds the instructions for one protein, or one piece of RNA. Humans have roughly twenty thousand genes, but only one or two percent of our DNA codes for proteins. Click the genes on this chromosome to see what they do.
s8: How does a gene become a body part? First, the cell copies the gene into messenger RNA. That's transcription. Then a ribosome reads the message three letters at a time. Each three letter codon picks one amino acid. Change the DNA and watch the protein change!
s9: A mutation is a change in the DNA letters. Some do nothing, some swap one amino acid, and some break the protein. In sickle cell disease, a single letter change in the hemoglobin gene bends red blood cells. Try the different mutations and compare.
s10: You carry two copies of most genes, called alleles, one from each parent. A dominant allele can hide a recessive one. Use the Punnett square to cross parents and see the odds. Then solve the calico cat mystery, which involves the X chromosome!
s11: DNA connects all life. Humans share about ninety nine percent of their DNA with chimpanzees, and many of our genes have a version even in a banana. Click an animal to see its chromosomes and a trait gene we have in common.
s12: Final mission! Answer the questions to earn the rank of DNA Master. Then copy your cheat sheet to keep. Remember: DNA is a code, genes are recipes, chromosomes are the packed volumes, and you are a unique combination. Great work, scientist!
